Empirical Research Plan: “Product-Standards Shock and Firms’ Export Margins”

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
-------------------------------------------------
Chosen method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD), supplemented with “difference-in-discontinuities” (RD-DID) for dynamic effects.

Justification  
• The policy created a verifiable, single dimensional compliance threshold (e.g., maximum pesticide residue, minimum safety rating).  
• Firms/products whose pre-policy compliance measure lies just above the cutoff can keep exporting without adjustment; those just below must upgrade or exit—the classic RD set-up.  
• Because we observe several years before and after the reform, we can difference pre-post outcomes on either side of the cutoff to net out any pre-existing discontinuity (difference-in-RD).  
• RD exploits quasi-random assignment in a narrow window around the cutoff, delivering local causal effects on both extensive (export participation) and intensive (export value/volume) margins.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
-------------------------------------------------
Running variable (R): Pre-policy compliance score for each firm–product (e.g., mg/kg of chemical, quality rating).  
Cutoff (c): The new statutory threshold introduced in year T₀ (e.g., R ≤ c is non-compliant).  

Treatment indicator (D):  
Dᵢ = 1 if Rᵢ ≤ c (non-compliant → forced to adjust)  
Dᵢ = 0 if Rᵢ > c (already compliant)  

Treatment timing: policy becomes effective in fiscal year T₀. We keep observations within ±h of the cutoff, observed in years T ∈ {T₀-k … T₀+m}.

Groups  
• Treated: firm-products with R just below c (within bandwidth h).  
• Control: firm-products with R just above c (within h).

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at R=c in absence of treatment.  
Plausible: the standard was exogenously set; firms could not perfectly choose R with fine precision.

A2. No precise manipulation of R around c.  
Plausible because R is measured pre-policy or comes from 3rd-party lab tests; still testable with McCrary density test.

A3. Local Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers within bandwidth).  
Reasonable: adapting below the cutoff does not directly change costs for firms just above the cutoff in short run; we will probe via alternative bandwidths.

A4. Parallel trends in “difference-in-discontinuities” version (pre-post continuity gap stable absent policy).  
Check with event-time leads to show no pre-trend discontinuity.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
-------------------------------------------------
1. Sorting / manipulation of R  
   • Conduct McCrary density test.  
   • Verify pre-policy R is measured before the reform was announced (no anticipatory gaming).  
   • Use audit/inspection data as robustness.

2. Measurement error in R  
   • Use multiple sources or averaged lab tests.  
   • Instrument measured R with lagged inspection results and re-estimate.

3. Concurrent shocks (exchange-rate swing, other trade policy) that differentially hit low-quality products.  
   • Include product-year fixed effects.  
   • Implement RD-DID: subtract pre-existing discontinuity to purge confounds.  
   • Placebo cutoffs at c±δ.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
-------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(rdrobust)
library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Load & Prepare Data ----
dt <- fread("firm_product_exports.csv")  # assumed wide file
# Key vars: firm_id, product_code, year, export_value, export_volume, compliance_score

# Policy year and cutoff
T0 <- 2015
c   <- 0.00        # example: 0 = new max residue

# Running variable
dt[, running := compliance_score - c]     # distance from threshold

# Treatment dummy (sharp RD)
dt[, treat := as.integer(running <= 0)]

# Post-policy dummy
dt[, post  := as.integer(year >= T0)]

# Outcomes
dt[, log_val := log1p(export_value)]
dt[, export_dummy := as.integer(export_value > 0)]

# Keep window h
h <- 0.05
dt_w <- dt[abs(running) <= h]

# ---- 2. Graphical RD ----
ggplot(dt_w[year==T0-1], aes(running, log_val)) +
  geom_point(alpha=.3) +
  geom_smooth(method="loess", span=.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=0, lty=2)

# ---- 3. Main RD (local linear) in post-policy years ----
out_main <- rdrobust(y = dt_w[post==1]$log_val,
                     x = dt_w[post==1]$running,
                     covs = dt_w[post==1][, .(log(export_volume+1))])
summary(out_main)

# ---- 4. Difference-in-RD (RD-DID) ----
feols(log_val ~ treat*post | firm_id + product_code + year,
      data = dt_w, cluster = ~firm_id)

# ---- 5. Robustness: alternative bandwidth ----
for (h_alt in c(0.03, 0.07)) {
  dt_tmp <- dt[abs(running) <= h_alt]
  res <- rdrobust(y = dt_tmp[post==1]$log_val,
                  x = dt_tmp[post==1]$running)
  print(paste("Bandwidth:", h_alt))
  print(summary(res)$coef[1,])   # treatment effect
}

# ---- 6. Density test ----
rddensity(dt$running, c = 0)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
-------------------------------------------------
• Extensive margin: negative—firms just below the cutoff face new fixed compliance costs and some will exit; expect drop in probability of exporting by 5-10 p.p. within the window.  
• Intensive margin: conditional on survival, effect may be weakly positive (less competition) or zero; theory suggests +3-5 % in surviving firms’ export value.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
-------------------------------------------------
C1: Visible continuity of pre-treatment outcomes at cutoff? … 1  
C2: No bunching/manipulation around cutoff (McCrary test)? … 1  
C3: Covariate balance within bandwidth? … 1  
C4: Robust to bandwidth & polynomial order choices? … 0.5  
C5: Placebo cutoffs/time falsification checks? … 1  

Total ≈ 4.5 / 5 → Strong, but bandwidth sensitivity needs scrutiny.
